prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: [val] Sparse tall row · Server inventory (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Host" · longest unbreakable word 43px · one-line width 57px
  col 2: header "Role" · longest unbreakable word 52px · one-line width 52px
  col 3: header "Zone" · longest unbreakable word 35px · one-line width 69px
  col 4: header "CPU" · longest unbreakable word 28px · one-line width 28px
  col 5: header "Status" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 6: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 57px · one-line width 1243px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 634px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 633px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"The narrow Notes column turns one entry into a very tall, fragmented block, separating the surrounding server rows and making the table hard to scan."},"B":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The note has room to read, but every zone identifier wraps, making routine rows taller and slowing comparison across servers."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Host and zone identifiers stay intact, the compact fields are easy to compare, and Notes has enough width to keep the exceptional row reasonably short."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"Identifiers stay intact and the columns read clearly, though the extra space in the short fields leaves Notes narrower and its row taller than in C."},"E":{"grade":"poor","why":"Zone identifiers wrap over three lines and some host names split, disrupting nearly every row despite the generous Notes width."}},"best":["C"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"The images are small, so subtle differences in spacing are harder to judge."}
